        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The paper focuses on adapting an evidence-based spelling intervention into a serious game for children with dyslexia. The design process is driven by linguistic error analysis, creation of targeted exercise types, and difficulty levels to improve spelling performance, indicating a primarily utilitarian, therapeutic goal with game elements layered on, rather than starting from entertainment or co-design workshops.
